decks.domain: Reckless and aggressive driving, emergencies and crashes

cards.front: What is reckless driving, and does it require intent?
cards.back: Reckless driving means operating a vehicle in a way that endangers people or property, whether or not it is intentional.

cards.front: What can a reckless driving conviction add to your record?
cards.back: If an officer sees your driving as endangering a person or property, including another vehicle, you can be charged under the reckless driving statute and face up to eight points on your record if convicted.

cards.front: When can tailgating or running a red light be treated as aggressive driving?
cards.back: Tailgating, passing on the shoulder or running a red light can be treated as aggressive when an officer believes it was willful and endangered others, and so can a mix of speeding, cutting off, swerving, honking, flashing lights, yelling and rude gestures.

cards.front: How does reckless driving differ from aggressive driving?
cards.back: Reckless driving needs no intent, only danger to people or property, while aggressive driving turns on willful acts that put others in danger.

cards.front: Which acts toward another motorist can bring criminal charges beyond reckless driving?
cards.back: Showing a weapon to another motorist, bumping or ramming a vehicle, or chasing a vehicle at high speed can bring criminal charges beyond reckless driving.

decks.domain: Reckless and aggressive driving, emergencies and crashes

cards.front: How should you protect yourself from an aggressive driver?
cards.back: To protect yourself from an aggressive driver, do not engage: avoid eye contact, do not respond in kind, back off and let the driver go.

cards.front: What are warning signs that you may be becoming an aggressive driver?
cards.back: Anyone can become an aggressive driver; warning signs include insulting other drivers, blocking merges or passing, tailgating to push someone, angry speeding, running controls out of anger, honking or yelling, gestures, pursuing or ramming, getting out to confront, or thinking about attacking.

cards.front: What does answering yes to a couple of the self-check questions mean?
cards.back: Answering yes to even a couple of the self-check questions means you may be at risk of becoming an aggressive driver.

cards.front: How can you avoid becoming an aggressive driver?
cards.back: To avoid becoming aggressive, leave early, expect others to make mistakes, stay calm, keep anger from elsewhere out of your driving and let people merge even if they were rude.

decks.domain: Reckless and aggressive driving, emergencies and crashes

cards.front: When a crash seems likely, is there usually anything you can do?
cards.back: When a crash seems likely, many drivers panic, yet there is almost always something you can do to avoid it or lessen its results.

cards.front: What are the three ways to avoid a collision?
cards.back: The three ways to avoid a collision are to slow down or stop, to turn, or to speed up.

cards.front: Is it usually faster to turn or to stop, and how should you steer around a hazard?
cards.back: You can usually turn a vehicle faster than you can stop it, so steer around a hazard if that will not cause another crash, gripping the wheel with both hands and staying ready to control the car afterward.

cards.front: Is leaving the road better or worse than a head-on collision?
cards.back: Leaving the road is generally a better outcome than a head-on collision with another vehicle.

cards.front: When can accelerating be the way out of danger?
cards.back: Accelerating out of danger can be the answer when another vehicle is about to strike your side or rear and the road ahead is open; slow back down afterward.

cards.front: When and where should you watch most carefully for animals?
cards.back: Watch for animals especially in rural and mountain areas and between dusk and dawn, when about ninety percent of deer and elk crashes happen, and slow down and look on entering a marked animal crossing.
cards.memory_hook: dusk to dawn, watch for deer

cards.front: Why might hitting a large animal be safer than swerving drastically?
cards.back: A drastic swerve to miss a large animal can cause loss of control and a worse crash, so hitting the animal may be the safest choice; focus on keeping control before, during and after impact.

cards.front: Which is more dangerous: swerving hard to miss a large animal or hitting it?
cards.back: Swerving hard to miss a large animal can be more dangerous than hitting it, and running off the road beats a head-on crash.

decks.domain: Reckless and aggressive driving, emergencies and crashes

cards.front: How do you make an emergency stop with anti-lock brakes?
cards.back: To stop fast with anti-lock brakes, press hard and firmly and keep the pedal down even if it pushes back, since ABS works only while the pedal is pressed.

cards.front: How do you make an emergency stop without anti-lock brakes?
cards.back: To stop fast without anti-lock brakes, brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels; if they lock and you skid, ease off slightly, then brake again once the skid stops, repeating until stopped.

cards.front: How does emergency braking differ with and without ABS?
cards.back: Emergency braking is opposite by brake type: with ABS keep firm pressure and never let up, without ABS brake just short of lockup and ease off if you skid.

cards.front: What do anti-lock brakes let you do while braking?
cards.back: Anti-lock brakes let you steer while braking without skidding, which helps when you must turn and slow at once.

cards.front: How do you make an evasive turn without anti-lock brakes?
cards.back: Without anti-lock brakes, brake to slow somewhat, then release the brake before the evasive turn, and do not lock the front wheels or turn so sharply that the car only plows ahead.

cards.front: In what order do you brake and steer for an evasive turn without ABS?
cards.back: Without ABS, an emergency turn is done in sequence: brake to slow, release the brake, then steer away, never locking the front wheels.

decks.domain: Reckless and aggressive driving, emergencies and crashes

cards.front: What greatly reduces the chance of a vehicle failure?
cards.back: Following the maintenance schedule in the owner's manual greatly reduces the chance of a vehicle failure.

cards.front: What should you do if your brakes fail?
cards.back: If the brakes fail, lift off the gas and pump the pedal; if that fails, apply the parking brake slowly, ready to release it if you skid, then shift to lower gears, find a safe spot off the road and do not drive on without brakes.

cards.front: What should you do if the gas pedal jams?
cards.back: If the gas pedal jams, keep your eyes on the road, shift to neutral quickly, pull off when safe and turn off the engine.

cards.front: How does the response to brake failure differ from a jammed gas pedal?
cards.back: Brake failure starts with pumping the pedal, then the parking brake applied slowly, then lower gears; a jammed gas pedal calls for shifting to neutral.

cards.front: What should you do in a tire blowout?
cards.back: In a tire blowout, grip the wheel tightly, keep going straight, take your foot off the gas, brake lightly and slow gradually, then pull off the road somewhere safe.

cards.front: Should you brake hard in a tire blowout?
cards.back: A blowout calls for gentle braking while holding straight, not hard braking or an immediate stop on the road.

cards.front: What happens to steering and brakes if power fails, and what do you do?
cards.back: If power fails, hold the wheel firmly and pull off the road; steering will be hard but possible, and the brakes still work with much harder pressure.

cards.front: What should you do if your headlights fail?
cards.back: If headlights fail, pull off as soon as possible, try the switch a few times, and if that does not work use the emergency flashers, turn signals or fog lights.

decks.domain: Reckless and aggressive driving, emergencies and crashes

cards.front: What must you show law enforcement after a crash?
cards.back: After a crash you must show proof of insurance to law enforcement, either at the scene or at the police station.

cards.front: Who must report an injury crash if the driver cannot?
cards.back: If the driver cannot physically report an injury crash, a passenger must report it and, if law enforcement directs, stay at the scene until officers arrive.

cards.front: What must you do after a crash?
cards.back: After a crash, stop at once and never leave, check for injuries and give reasonable help where practical, call law enforcement and emergency services, and exchange names, addresses, phone numbers, registration and insurance.

cards.front: What should you do if you hit a parked car and cannot find the owner?
cards.back: If you hit a parked car and cannot find its owner, call law enforcement and leave a note where the owner will find it.

decks.domain: Reckless and aggressive driving, emergencies and crashes

cards.front: What do drivers do in a qualifying crash during Accident Alert Status?
cards.back: During Accident Alert Status, when severe weather keeps officers from answering all crashes, drivers in a crash with no alcohol, drugs or injuries and drivable vehicles exchange information and must file a report within twenty-four hours.

cards.front: What does the Move It Law require after a minor divided-highway crash?
cards.back: Under the Move It Law, after a minor divided-highway crash with drivable vehicles and no injuries, drugs or alcohol, drivers must get the vehicles off the highway, and police and insurers will not penalize them for it.

cards.front: How does the Move It Law differ from Accident Alert Status?
cards.back: When vehicles are drivable and neither injuries nor drugs or alcohol are involved, the Move It Law requires clearing a minor divided-highway crash off the road, whereas Accident Alert Status requires exchanging details and reporting within twenty-four hours.

cards.front: What does the Move Over Law require for a stopped vehicle with hazards flashing?
cards.back: The Move Over Law requires moving over one lane, when safe, for any stopped vehicle on a highway with hazards flashing; if that is unsafe or the road has one lane each way, slow to at least twenty miles per hour under the posted limit.

cards.front: What does the Move Over Law require for a stationary highway vehicle with hazards flashing?
cards.back: For any stationary highway vehicle flashing its hazards, the Move Over Law requires moving over one lane when safe, or slowing to at least twenty miles per hour below the posted speed limit if unsafe or on a road with one lane each way.

decks.domain: Reckless and aggressive driving, emergencies and crashes

cards.front: What do Good Samaritan laws expect, and how do they protect rescuers?
cards.back: Good Samaritan laws encourage helping in emergencies and expect common sense and reasonable skill within your training; acting as a reasonable, prudent person generally protects a rescuer from being sued and held financially responsible.

cards.front: How does a reasonable rescuer act at an emergency?
cards.back: A reasonable rescuer moves a victim only if life is in danger, asks a conscious victim before helping, checks for life-threatening problems first, calls for professional help and keeps giving care until trained help arrives.

cards.front: What happens if you say yes to organ, eye and tissue donation when licensing?
cards.back: When applying for or renewing a license, permit or ID you are asked whether to register as an organ, eye and tissue donor; a yes puts a heart with a Y on the card and adds you to the Donate Life Colorado registry until you change it.

cards.front: What is the voluntary gift you are asked about when licensing?
cards.back: You are also asked whether to make a voluntary gift to the organ and tissue donation awareness fund named for Emily Keyes and John W. Buckner, which pays for public outreach and education.

recap_hooks.text: Reckless driving needs no intent; aggressive driving is willful danger to others.
Do not engage with aggressive drivers, know your own warning signs, and leave early to stay calm.
Stop, turn or speed up to avoid a collision; leaving the road beats a head-on crash.
Do not swerve drastically for a large animal.
With ABS press hard and hold; without ABS brake short of lockup and release before an evasive turn.
Pump failed brakes, shift to neutral for a jammed pedal, and brake gently in a blowout.
After a crash, stop, help, call and exchange information, and show proof of insurance.
Move over a lane for stopped vehicles with hazards, or slow to at least twenty under the limit.
Good Samaritan laws protect reasonable rescuers who ask, check, call and stay.

merges.justification: sec15-F06 (reporting an aggressive driver to the State Patrol line) is the follow-on step to sec15-F05 (do not engage with an aggressive driver); its accepted wording contains an asterisk symbol that cannot be spoken as a card back, so the sec15-F05 card carries both in the module and the fact stays taught in the lesson and exam bank.
